vial.e: From Middle English vial, viole, a variant of fiole, phiole, phial (“small bowl or cup for liquids, etc.; flask”): see further at phial.
vial.g: A glass or plastic vessel or bottle, especially a small tube-shaped bottle used to store medicine, perfume or other chemicals.

vicinity.e: From vicine + -ity, from Latin vīcīnitās (“neighborhood”) (compare French vicinité), from vīcīnus (“neighbor”) (compare French voisin), from vīcus (“village”).
vicinity.g: Proximity; the state of being near.

vicious.e: From Middle English vicious, from Anglo-Norman vicious, (modern French vicieux), from Latin vitiōsus, from vitium (“fault, vice”). Equivalent to vice + -ous.

viciously.e: From Middle English viciously; equivalent to vicious + -ly.
viciously.g: In a vicious manner; ferociously or maliciously.

victim.e: From Middle French victime, from Latin victima (“sacrificial animal”). Although this root and victor drive from homophonous PIE roots, they are traditionally reconstructed as separate words and thus not cognates.
victim.g: One that is harmed—killed, injured, subjected to oppression, deceit, or otherwise adversely affected—by someone or something, especially ano

victorious.e: Borrowed from Latin victōriōsus, from victōria (“victory”), from victor (“conqueror”).
victorious.g: Being the winner in a contest, struggle, war, etc.

victory.e: The English word is analysable as victor + -y (suffix forming abstract nouns denoting a condition, quality, or state), and displaced Middle English siȝe, sye. The interjection is derived from the noun. Tamil வெற்றி (veṟṟi) (pronounced roughly like "vetri") is a false cognate.
victory.g: The condition or state of having won a battle or competition, or having succeeded in an effort; (countable) an instance of this.

victory.e: From Middle English victorien (“to overcome, vanquish”), from Old French victorier, or from Medieval Latin victōriāre, from Latin victōria (noun); see further at etymology 1.
victory.g: To defeat or triumph over (someone or something).

victual.e: From Middle English vitaile, vitaylle (“food; food and drink, especially as needed for sustenance; (usually in the plural) food and drink stores or supplies; rations; provision of food and drink as a military stipend; crops”).
victual.g: Food fit for human (or occasionally animal) consumption.

victual.e: From Middle English vitailen (“to provide (someone, a castle, a ship, etc., or oneself) with supplies of food, drink, or other needs; (figuratively) to load (a ship with troops and materiel); to fortify, nourish”), from Anglo-Norman vitailer, vitailler, and Old French vitailler, victuailler.
victual.g: To provide (military troops, a place, a ship, etc., or oneself) with a stock of victuals or food; to provision.

view.e: From Middle English vewe, from Anglo-Norman vewe, from Old French veue f (French vue f), feminine past participle of veoir (“to see”) (French voir).

vigil.e: From Middle English vigile (“a devotional watching”), from Old French vigile, from Latin vigilia (“wakefulness, watch”), from vigil (“awake”), from Proto-Indo-European *weǵ- (“to be strong, lively, awake”).
vigil.g: An instance of keeping awake during normal sleeping hours, especially to keep watch or pray.

vigilant.e: From French vigilant or its source, Latin vigilans, present participle of vigilare (“stay awake”), from vigil (“awake”).
vigilant.g: Watchful, especially for danger or disorder; alert; wary.

vigorous.e: From Anglo-Norman vigrus, from Old French vigoros (French vigoureux), from Medieval Latin vigorosus, from Latin vigor.

vile.e: From Middle English vile, vyle, vyl, from Anglo-Norman ville, Old French vil, vile, from Latin vīlis.

vilely.e: From Middle English vyly, vileliche, fijlliche, villiche, equivalent to vile + -ly.
vilely.g: In a vile manner, evilly, despicably.

vilify.e: From Late Latin vīlificāre (“vilify”). Equivalent to vile + -ify.
vilify.g: To say defamatory things about someone or something; to speak ill of.

village.e: From Middle English village, from Old French village, from Latin vīllāticus, ultimately from Latin villa (English villa). Broadly overtook Old English wic, þorp, and ham. The Philippine sense is due to its frequent use in the names of gated communities.
village.g: A rural habitation of size between a hamlet and a town.

vindicate.e: Borrowed from Latin vindicātus, perfect passive participle of vindicō (“lay legal claim to something; set free; protect, avenge, punish”), from vim, accusative singular of vīs (“force, power”), + dīcō (“say; declare, state”).
vindicate.g: To clear of an accusation, suspicion or criticism.

vindication.e: From Late Middle English vendicacion, vyndicacion, vyndycacion (“assertion of a claim”), from Old French vindication (“revenge, vengeance”) (modern dialectal French vindication), or from Medieval Latin vendicātio, both from Latin vindicātiō (“avenging; defence, protection, vindication; punishment; etc.”), from vindicō (“to avenge; to take revenge on.
vindication.g: An act of asserting or maintaining; an assertion.

vine.e: From Middle English vyne, from Anglo-Norman vigne, from Vulgar Latin vīnia, from Latin vīnea (“vines in a vineyard”), from vīneus (“related to wine”), from vīnum (“wine”), from Proto-Italic *wīnom, from Proto-Indo-European *wóyh₁nom (“vine, wine”), from *weh₁y- (“to twist, wrap”).
vine.g: Any plant whose stem requires support and which climbs by tendrils or twining.

vinedresser.g: Someone who works in a vineyard.

vinegar.e: From Middle English vynegre, from Old French vinaigre from Old French vyn egre, based on Latin vīnum (“wine”) + Latin ācer (“sour”).
vinegar.g: A sour liquid formed by the fermentation of alcohol used as a condiment or preservative; a dilute solution of acetic acid.

vineyard.e: Equivalent to vine + yard; from Middle English vyneȝerd (circa 1300), following earlier Old English wīnġeard (“wine yard, vine yard”), with vine (from Old French vigne (“vine, vineyard”), from Latin vīnea) replacing native Old English wīn (“wine, vine”).
vineyard.g: A grape plantation, especially one used in the production of wine.

vintage.e: From Middle English vendage, vyndage, from Anglo-Norman vendenge, from Old French vendage, vendenge (cognate with French vendange), from Latin vindēmia (“a gathering of grapes, vintage”), from vīnum (“wine”) + dēmō (“take off or away, remove”), from de (“of; from, away from”) + emō (“take”).
vintage.g: The yield of grapes or wine from a vineyard or district during one season.

viol.e: Borrowed from Middle French viole, from Old French viol, from Old Occitan viola (modern Occitan viula), from Medieval Latin vitula (“stringed instrument”).
viol.g: A stringed instrument related to the violin family, but held in the lap between the legs like a cello, usually with C-holes, a flat back, a

violate.e: From Middle English violaten (“to defile, render impure”), from violat(e) (“defiled, desecrated”, also used as the past participle of violaten) + -en, borrowed from Latin violātus, perfect passive participle of violō (“to treat with violence (whether bodily or mental)”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix).
violate.g: To break or disregard (a rule or convention).

violate.e: From Middle English violat, from Classical Latin violātus.

violation.e: Borrowed from Middle French violation, from Latin violātiō (“injury, profanation”), from violō (“to treat with violence; to maltreat; to violate, defile, profane”). Morphologically violate + -ion.
violation.g: The act or an instance of violating or the condition of being violated.

violence.e: From Middle English violence, borrowed from Old French violence, a learned borrowing from Latin violentia, from violēns /violentus (“violent”) + -ia.

violent.e: From Middle English violent, from Old French violent, from Latin violentus, from vīs (“strength”). For the verb, compare French violenter.

violently.e: From Middle English violently; equivalent to violent + -ly.

viper.e: From Middle French vipere, from Old French vipre, from Latin vīpera, contracted from vīvipara f (“viviparous”, adj.), from vīvus (“alive”, adj.) + parere (“to bear”, verb).
viper.g: A venomous snake in the family Viperidae.

virgin.e: From Middle English virgine, from Old French virgine, from Latin virginem, accusative of virgō.
virgin.g: A person who has never had sexual intercourse, or (uncommonly) an animal that has never mated.

virginity.e: From Middle English virginite, from Old French virginite, from Latin virginitas. Equivalent to virgin + -ity.
virginity.g: The state or characteristic of being a virgin.

virility.e: From virile + -ity, from Middle French virilité, from Latin virīlitās.

virtue.e: From Middle English vertu, virtue, borrowed from Anglo-Norman vertu, virtu, from Latin virtus (“manliness, bravery, worth, moral excellence”), from vir (“man”). In this sense, displaced Old English cræft, whence Modern English craft.
virtue.g: The idea of all that is good or excellent (in every sense of those terms) in a human being, collectively instantiated by a varying number of

virtuous.e: From Middle English vertuous, borrowed from Anglo-Norman vertuous, vertous, ultimately from Late Latin virtuōsus, from Latin virtūs. By surface analysis, virtue + -ous.
virtuous.g: Full of virtue; having excellent moral character.

virtuously.e: From Middle English vertuously; equivalent to virtuous + -ly.

visage.e: From Middle English visage, from Anglo-Norman visage, from Vulgar Latin *vīsāticum, derived from Latin vīsus (“appearance, sight”), derived from vidēre (“to see”).

visible.e: From Middle English visible, from Old French visible, from Late Latin visibilis (“that may be seen”), from Latin videre (“to see”), past participle visus; see vision.

vision.e: From Middle English visioun, from Anglo-Norman visioun, from Old French vision, from Latin vīsiō (“vision, seeing”), noun of action from the perfect passive participle visus (“that which is seen”), from the verb videō (“to see”) + action noun suffix -iō.
vision.g: The sense or ability of sight.

visit.e: From Middle English visiten, from Old French visiter, from Latin vīsitō, frequentative of vīsō (“behold, survey”), from videō (“see”).
visit.g: To habitually go to (someone in distress, sickness etc.) to comfort them. (Now generally merged into later senses, below.)

visitation.e: From Anglo-Norman visitacioun, from Old French visitacion, from Latin vīsitātiō. By surface analysis, visit + -ation.
visitation.g: The act of visiting, or an instance of being visited.

visitor.e: Partly from Middle English visiter, visitere, equivalent to visit + -er; and partly from Middle English visitour, from Anglo-Norman visitour, from Old French visetëor. By surface analysis, visit + -or.
visitor.g: Someone who visits someone else; someone staying as a guest.

vitality.e: From vital + -ity, from Middle French vitalité, from Latin vitalitas (“vital force, life”), from vitalis (“vital”); see vital.
vitality.g: The capacity to live and develop.
